title: An Ultra-Modern Outreach Workflow You Can Use TODAY
speakers_and_attribution: Pete Crowley introduces himself as head of growth at the company captioned variously as rbb/RB Tob, understood contextually as RB2B, and hosts in Adam Robinson's absence. Ryan Tully introduces himself as a Pitch Lane co-founder and supplies the product demonstration, founder history and most tactical recommendations. Adam does not speak in the supplied transcript. References to Adam's leave, earlier outbound commentary, Jasper office arrangement and inspiration are Pete's secondhand statements. Audience questions and feedback are relayed by the speakers. Speaker assignments follow introductions and conversational turns because the automatic captions are not diarized; company and personal names may contain transcription errors.
summary: Pete Crowley and Pitch Lane co-founder Ryan Tully demonstrate an outreach workflow combining a creative lead magnet, visitor identification, automated personalized video and LinkedIn or email follow-up. They emphasize short scripts, audience-dependent selling approaches, camera presence, targeting and action-triggered follow-up. The final third covers Ryan's inexpensive but unreliable prototype, customer evidence that persuaded him to continue, meeting his technical co-founder through outbound, partnerships and early-stage customer discovery. This source provides guest and host context for Adam's wiki, but no direct evidence of Adam's own beliefs or achievements.

key_learnings.claim: Pete frames outbound as a channel whose effective tactics are changing, with older high-volume approaches losing effectiveness for many users.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: Pete references prior commentary by Adam but presents this position as his and Ryan's; it does not establish Adam's precise view.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan argues that AI-assisted list building and personalization are bringing scalable outreach closer to the relevance previously associated with manual sales work.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A guest's market interpretation at the time of the webinar, without comparative performance evidence.

key_learnings.claim: A lead magnet can offer entertainment as well as practical information, provided it has some connection to the company's audience or product category.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: Pete explicitly doubts that the humorous LinkedIn roast will necessarily generate many high-intent leads; the demonstration is meant to inspire creativity.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan's roast demonstration uses a form webhook into Clay, LinkedIn contact enrichment, conditional AI generation and downstream delivery tools to create an automated experience without substantial coding skill.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: Describes Ryan's demonstration, not Adam's implementation. The enrichment provider's name is unclear in the captions.

key_learnings.claim: AI can support qualification and relevant message generation before leads enter a video-personalization system.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: Presented as available workflow possibilities; no qualification accuracy or conversion outcomes are supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan positions guides, checklists, free micro-tools and humorous experiences as routes to attracting relevant website visitors, then proposes visitor identification and video follow-up to convert that engagement.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A proposed funnel involving RB2B and Pitch Lane; visiting a lead magnet does not establish purchase intent.

key_learnings.claim: Pete explains that visitor identification can complement both gated and ungated content, including attempts to identify visitors who do not submit a form.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: The discussion supplies no identification coverage, accuracy or eligibility limits.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan deliberately chooses a simple LinkedIn workflow so participants can test quickly without the email warmup delays and multiple purchases he associates with complicated webinar demonstrations.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A design choice for this demonstration; the stated setup time is an estimate and assumes the necessary accounts and inputs.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan recommends placing the dynamic section at the start of a video, using the prospect's website or LinkedIn profile to make the opening feel personally relevant.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: The demonstrated personalization changes visual context around a reusable recording; it does not show a fresh individual analysis for every prospect.

key_learnings.claim: Keep the whole outreach video short and simple: explain the reason for contacting the person, who is speaking, why it matters and the next step, while preserving a natural human presentation.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: Ryan's creative guidance, without a tested ideal duration; he discourages unnecessary grooming or performance polish.

key_learnings.claim: For visitors already somewhat familiar with the company, Ryan recommends a direct sequence of pain-point question, social proof and call to action.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: The recommendation assumes prior exposure to the website or lead magnet; it is not presented as the right script for every cold audience.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan says direct pitches tend to suit SMB buyers who can decide quickly, while enterprise outreach often benefits from relationship building and longer nurturing.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A generalization from Ryan's experience, not a universal segmentation rule or a controlled comparison.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan adjusts outreach goals when relationships have value beyond an immediate sale; with sales leaders, a potential podcast invitation can make relationship building more useful than a hard pitch.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: Ryan describes uncertainty and variation in his own preference rather than settling on one permanently superior approach.

key_learnings.claim: Pitch Lane's demonstration records scrolling and screen-change timing once so its servers can recreate those actions over each prospect's website.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A product capability demonstrated as of this source; the transcript alone cannot verify visual output quality.

key_learnings.claim: The demonstrated integration sends identified visitors from RB2B into Pitch Lane using an endpoint and test event, after which rendered videos can be moved into a sequencing tool.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: The integration into Pitch Lane is demonstrated, but delivery into a LinkedIn campaign still needs an export/import step or additional automation.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan recommends starting with routine CSV exports if necessary and adding a video-rendered webhook or Zapier connection when greater automation is useful.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: This is a practical simplicity tradeoff; CSV handling is not fully automated and relies on ongoing operator action.

key_learnings.claim: Pete prefers daily follow-up processing so a website visitor receives the personalized video while the visit remains recent, and says more automatic profile-group routing is still being developed.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: The roughly 24-hour timing is a recommendation, not a measured service level; planned routing improvements should not be treated as shipped.

key_learnings.claim: Pete recommends aligning scripts and windows near the camera, rehearsing a few clear sentences and using a decent background so a reusable outreach recording feels attentive and understandable.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: Production advice from Pete; no measured causal effect on campaign performance is provided.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan uses a webcam positioned over the middle of the screen to preserve apparent eye contact while reading a script or watching a sales-call participant's reactions.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A personal equipment practice. His preceding claims about studies and human attention are not sourced in the webinar.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan favors outreach that changes after a prospect takes an action; his example sends video-view notifications into Slack, prompting a salesperson or founder to connect on LinkedIn.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: The associated meeting improvements are Ryan's unverified reports, with no denominator or measurement period.

key_learnings.claim: A video view can trigger a personal email, LinkedIn connection or phone call; Ryan says he has even called a prospect while the prospect was watching.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: This is Ryan's tactic and anecdote, not evidence that every audience welcomes immediate cross-channel contact.

key_learnings.claim: Pete distinguishes video attention from replies: his own thumbnail messages reportedly drew very high viewing, while an attendee's custom videos received no responses.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley, relaying attendee Connie's experience
key_learnings.caveat: Two anecdotes without sample sizes; the attendee's result is relayed by Pete rather than directly supplied as an attributed transcript turn.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan's early sales work led him to look for large, obvious improvements rather than small A/B-test gains when data was scarce.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: His numerical contrasts are rhetorical descriptions of desired improvement, not measured lift.

key_learnings.claim: An unreliable prototype can still test demand: Ryan's first version crashed and rendered slowly, but it let him run LinkedIn campaigns and find initial interest.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A historical Pitch Lane example; it does not establish acceptable reliability for a mature customer-facing product.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan nearly abandoned Pitch Lane for another job, then committed after a friend's employer-required before-and-after evaluation supplied a persuasive first case study.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: The study and comparison are described by Ryan, not shown in the transcript; the decision relied heavily on one early customer context.

key_learnings.claim: Pete argues that an early bootstrapped founder may reasonably act on a small but credible customer signal when broad data is unavailable, while explicitly acknowledging anecdotal evidence and possible outliers.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: Pete's interpretation of Ryan's decision, not Adam's position or a statistical validation of the evidence.

key_learnings.claim: Ryan attributes part of Pitch Lane's progress to partnerships and complementary improvements in data, targeting and sending tools, because better inputs and distribution improve the usefulness of its video layer.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: A qualitative explanation of Pitch Lane's progress; several partner names are unclear in the automatic captions.

key_learnings.claim: Pete emphasizes selecting relevant leads and tailoring messages to different groups at scale as the basis for effective campaigns.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: A host recommendation without comparative campaign data.

key_learnings.claim: Pete encourages sharing workflows on LinkedIn and requesting feedback from peers and the presenters as a practical way to improve outreach.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: A suggested feedback practice; it does not establish an approved building-in-public philosophy for Adam.

key_learnings.claim: For founders still discovering their market, Ryan recommends openly explaining their situation, relevant experience and uncertainty, then inviting potential customers to explore their needs.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully
key_learnings.caveat: His example about leaving a marketing executive role is a hypothetical script, not his biography. This advice concerns market discovery, not established targeting.

key_learnings.claim: Pete recalls that asking for product advice produced the most meetings in a previous early-stage company, after his team borrowed the approach from another founder's outreach.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: The company is unnamed and described as helping e-commerce businesses with shipping; it must not be assigned to Adam or RB2B.

key_learnings.claim: When an email conversation stalls, Ryan recommends prompt phone follow-up after a reply, while Pete suggests testing a more personal channel and revising the follow-up message.
key_learnings.speaker: Ryan Tully and Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: Synthesis of their distinct recommendations. They have little diagnostic detail about the attendee's nearshoring campaign and present no measured results for the proposed changes.

key_learnings.claim: Pete suggests learning from the post-webinar customer experience by observing Pitch Lane's subsequent messages, videos and sales touchpoints.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete Crowley
key_learnings.caveat: An invitation to study an expected follow-up sequence; the sequence and its results are not included in this transcript.

backstory_and_values.claim: Pete says he is filling in for Adam during leave and that Adam is expected to return the following week.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Pete Crowley
backstory_and_values.caveat: Secondhand Adam context. The captions say 'fraternity leave'; the intended leave type cannot be established from the text alone.

backstory_and_values.claim: Ryan says he wanted to run a business from childhood and enjoyed watching the UK entrepreneurship program Dragon's Den.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully

backstory_and_values.claim: At university, Ryan worked on a new plastic-recycling approach with a social enterprise in India, intending to help create employment, despite lacking a directly relevant technical background.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully
backstory_and_values.caveat: The location is captioned 'goodat' and is uncertain. Ryan says the pandemic disrupted the project in his final year, but gives no calendar year or achieved impact.

backstory_and_values.claim: Ryan chose a very early-stage startup as its first hire after the university project ended; by his start date it had pivoted from a bank-linked consumer carbon-footprint app to B2B, and he was tasked with learning outbound and sales.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully
backstory_and_values.caveat: The employer is unnamed. Ryan says he was given Y Combinator training materials; this does not independently establish the company's accelerator status.

backstory_and_values.claim: After a later startup job proved a poor fit, Ryan decided to act on his business ambition rather than remain someone who only wanted to start a company.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully
backstory_and_values.caveat: A concrete decision and motivation in Ryan's account; it is not evidence of Adam's values.

backstory_and_values.claim: Ryan spent money he considered significant on an outsourced first prototype, considered returning to employment, and then chose to continue after receiving strong customer evidence.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully
backstory_and_values.caveat: Shows Ryan's decision changing in response to evidence; it should not be simplified into unconditional persistence.

backstory_and_values.claim: Ryan met his eventual technical co-founder Patrick through a LinkedIn event outreach campaign that otherwise generated poorly qualified connections.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully
backstory_and_values.caveat: Patrick's surname and the event date are not supplied. Ryan praises the complementary coding ability; no equity or employment arrangement is discussed.

backstory_and_values.claim: Pete describes Ryan as a bootstrapped founder with a small team and credits Pitch Lane's product and proactive co-marketing ideas with helping secure the collaboration.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Pete Crowley
backstory_and_values.caveat: Host characterization and praise, with no funding history, team count or measured co-marketing impact.

backstory_and_values.claim: Ryan says he personally gives extra consideration to people starting businesses, and recommends candidly communicating uncertainty when seeking early customer conversations.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Ryan Tully
backstory_and_values.caveat: A stated preference and recommendation from Ryan; it is not an approved author mission or voice claim.

backstory_and_values.claim: Pete says Adam rented a small workspace in Jasper's office, observed its growth and was inspired to take the business he calls 'retention' further.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Pete Crowley
backstory_and_values.caveat: Secondhand Adam backstory with no dates or concrete business outcomes. 'Retention' is not fully named here, and the workspace description is explicitly approximate.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Pete Crowley
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Contemporaneous product-status claim in a source published 2024-10-16; neither the precise launch date nor the recording date is stated.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Guest company promotional self-report. Engagement definition, baseline, sample, customer cohort and measurement period are unspecified; this is not an Adam or RB2B result.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: A repetition of the earlier claim in sales copy, not an independent result; '2X increase' is colloquial and should not be converted into a different percentage interpretation.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Guest self-report apparently associated with his workflow; exact population, baseline, attribution method and period are absent.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Secondhand customer anecdote received 'yesterday' relative to the recording. Campaign period, denominator and counterfactual are unverified.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Pete Crowley
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical host self-report with no campaign dates, sample or measurement definition. Pete expressly says this was not a 100% response rate, and does not clearly assign the campaign to RB2B.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical guest self-report; the earlier caption truncates the currency, but Ryan later explicitly says '200 pound.' This is one prototype expense, not total funding, burn or development cost.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Pitch Lane original prototype throughput: Ryan says a 1.5-minute video took roughly two minutes to generate sequentially, so 100 videos would take 200 minutes, with frequent crashes.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical prototype description and illustrative arithmetic; 200 minutes is not a benchmark for the later product and excludes any crash-related delay.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Early Pitch Lane comparison: Ryan recounts his best friend reporting approximately 2–3× the performance of the friend's company's existing sequences.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical secondhand report. The outcome metric, company, sample and dates are unspecified. Ryan says the employer required a documented before-and-after comparison, but that documentation is not supplied.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Pitch Lane technical co-founder recruitment: Ryan says one qualified connection from an otherwise unsuccessful LinkedIn event campaign became his co-founder Patrick.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical guest self-report; total outreach volume and qualification criteria are missing. This is not a customer-acquisition conversion rate.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Ryan's earlier unnamed employer: he describes himself as its first hire and says approximately two months elapsed between getting the job and starting, during which the company pivoted to B2B.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical personal chronology, with no calendar dates. 'First hire' does not establish total team size, founder count or employment classification.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Workflow setup estimate: Ryan says viewers should be able to reproduce the demonstrated setup in about 15 minutes or less, contrasting it with email warmup waits of roughly two weeks.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: An estimated implementation time and illustrative comparison at the time of recording, not measured onboarding performance or a guarantee.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Website-visitor follow-up target: Pete recommends daily handling so visitors receive a custom video within approximately 24 hours.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Pete Crowley
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Operational recommendation, not an achieved response-time metric or contractual service level.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Pitch Lane trial: Pete advertises 14 days of free access, while Ryan mentions free credits; Pete also describes free access to RB2B.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Pete Crowley and Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical offer descriptions at recording, not current pricing. Credit quantities, eligibility and the relationship between free credits and the trial are unspecified.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Reply follow-up target: Ryan recommends calling within five minutes of an email reply when possible.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: A proposed speed-to-contact target; no numerical response-rate lift or supporting study is supplied.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Early experimentation framing: Ryan contrasts a 5% improvement with a desired 500% improvement and calls video an order-of-magnitude improvement.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Ryan Tully
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Rhetorical comparisons, not measured performance. They should not be reconciled with or substituted for his separate 2× and 2–3× claims.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Programming dates: Pete says Adam will return on Tuesday for a conversation with Jasper's founder, and says this recording will be available the following morning.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Pete Crowley
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Plans relative to an undated recording, not confirmed event dates. The guest name is garbled as 'Dave Rogan Moser'; the publication timestamp must not be treated as the recording date.

tensions_and_corrections: Adam is absent throughout. None of Ryan's founder history, Pitch Lane performance claims or Pete's personal campaigns should be entered as Adam's self-reported achievements or beliefs.
Pete's reference to Adam discussing outbound being dead does not establish Adam's exact position; the spoken position developed here belongs to Pete and Ryan and concerns changing tactics.

The workflow is introduced as automated, but the simple version requires recurring CSV exports and imports. Full downstream delivery requires additional automation, and Pete says some profile routing is still in development.
The humorous roast attracts engagement, but Pete questions its likely purchase intent. Ryan presents it as a relevant creative demonstration rather than a proven high-intent acquisition channel.

Reusable video is presented as personal and relevant, but the demonstration changes prospect-specific visual context around a single recording. The sample script implies the sender reviewed the website; individual manual review is not established.
Ryan's preference for natural, minimally polished recording coexists with Pete's advice to rehearse and improve eye contact, articulation and background. Both favor clarity over elaborate production.

The 2× engagement claim, 30% meeting uplift, five customer meetings, nearly 100% viewing anecdote and early 2–3× sequence comparison refer to different speakers, outcomes and contexts. They cannot be combined into one performance narrative.
Ryan's 5%, 500% and order-of-magnitude language is rhetorical and numerically non-equivalent. Preserve it as emphasis rather than corrected or validated performance data.
High viewing does not imply replies or bookings. Pete explicitly separates viewing from response, and an attendee reports no response to custom videos.
Ryan shifts between hard selling and relationship building depending on audience and secondary goals. SMB-versus-enterprise differences are his experience-based tendencies, not universal rules.
Advice to target tightly later gives way to broad, candid exploratory outreach for founders who do not yet know their market. The boundary condition is the stage of customer discovery.

Ryan nearly stopped pursuing Pitch Lane; documented feedback from a trusted early user changed his decision. Pete acknowledges the limited sample and potential outlier problem while defending action under uncertainty.

The episode contains no Adam/RB2B ARR, revenue, profit, cash, funding or customer-count figures, and no exact Pitch Lane team size. Bootstrapping discussion does not include a substantive VC comparison.
Automatic captions vary RB2B and Pitch Lane spellings and garble some names, places and the leave description. Uncertain details have not been silently converted into verified facts.
Publication, capture and event dates are distinct. Relative references such as yesterday, next Tuesday and tomorrow morning remain anchored to the recording rather than assigned calendar dates.
This is internal research from a publicly accessible source; it does not establish clearance for reuse in new public copy or an approved Adam voice or mission.
